title: Ramana Maharshi (Who Am I?)
hook: a stick that tends a fire until the fire takes the stick

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramana Maharshi and his question, who am I?: body, senses, breath and mind set aside, and awareness left over. Did you catch yourself owning something, my this, my that? Your line was who's doing the owning. Day nine hundred fifty.

At a cremation fire, someone tends the flames with a long stick, pushing the wood in, turning it so it burns through. It's a plain, sober job. And at the end, when everything has burned, the stick goes into the fire too. Ramana Maharshi takes that stick and puts it in the middle of Who Am I? It's his answer to a question the text raises plainly: what do you do with all these thoughts?
screen: `A STICK TENDS THE FIRE.` → `AT THE END, THE STICK BURNS TOO.` → `WHAT ABOUT ALL THESE THOUGHTS?`

segments.voice: Ramana's advice is short. When a thought comes up, don't follow it. Don't argue with it, either. Instead ask: to whom did this thought come? The answer arrives on its own: to me. Then ask: and who am I? That turns the mind back toward where it came from, he says, and the thought that started it all fades. Do it again with the next one. And the next. Each time, the question brings you home. Here's the reason it works, in his account. All the other thoughts hang on one thought: the thought I. Worry, plans, memories, all of them belong to someone. Follow the I back, and the rest has nothing to hang on. So the question who am I? does the job of the stick. It keeps turning the other thoughts into the fire. And at the end, Ramana says, it burns up too. Even the question doesn't stay. There's a second picture in the text. Somebody asks whether a seeker first needs to study and count all the categories that philosophers say make up the world and the person, sorting them one by one. Ramana says no. If you want to throw out the garbage, he says, you don't need to analyze it first. Just throw it out. That can sound blunt. It's also a relief. In his account, you don't have to map everything you are not before you ask who you are. You only have to ask. Tomorrow, the helps Ramana allows along the way: the breath, a name of God, and an elephant.
screen: `TO WHOM DID THIS THOUGHT COME? TO ME.` · `EVERY THOUGHT HANGS ON THE THOUGHT 'I'.` · `THE STICK BURNS AT THE END TOO.` · then, large: `NO NEED TO SORT THE GARBAGE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Wait for the first thought; it won't take long. When it comes, don't follow its story. Ask quietly: to whom did this come? Let the answer be there: to me. Then ask: who am I? and let the attention turn back, toward the one asking. Rest there until the next thought arrives, and do it again, as many times as it takes. No need to judge the thoughts or sort them. If you pray, you can let this turning home be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Ramana Maharshi. The teacher who said: when a thought comes, ask to whom it came, then ask who am I, and let the question burn up like the stick in the fire.
Your line: to whom did this come? Today, when one thought keeps circling back, don't untangle it. Ask once: to whom did this come? Day nine hundred fifty.

howItsDone: In self-inquiry as Ramana taught it, people meet each passing thought with 'to whom did this come?' and turn back toward the sense of 'I', in sitting practice and through the day.

fork.setup: you're sitting quietly and a worry pops up about tomorrow's meeting. what does Ramana say to do?
options: think it through until it's solved.
ask: to whom did this come? then: who am I?
push it down and think of something nicer.
fork.reveal: Ramana says not to pursue the thought but to ask to whom it came. the answer, 'to me', leads to 'who am I?', and the mind turns back to its source.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: aham, 'I'. Ramana teaches that every other thought hangs on the thought 'I'.

trapdoor: what you thought: self-inquiry means thinking hard about yourself.
what it means: it means not following thoughts, asking to whom they came, and turning back toward the I.
what a scholar hears: the stick that stirs the cremation fire and burns at the end, Ramana's picture for a question that dissolves itself.
recall: I'm in my own little well too

sources.ref: Who Am I? (Nan Yar), on inquiring 'to whom did this arise?' and the stick used to stir the burning pyre
Who Am I? (Nan Yar), on not needing to analyze the categories (tattvas), like garbage thrown out unexamined

notes: All paraphrase; modern English translations of Nan Yar are under copyright. Confirm the 'to whom? to me. who am I?' sequence, the funeral-pyre stick image, and the garbage image as described.
Cremation imagery is used plainly and soberly; a Keeper should confirm the tone is respectful.
The garbage passage is phrased in some versions as a question-and-answer about analyzing the tattvas or tendencies; confirm the framing 'whether you first need to sort out ... old tendencies'.

Editor pass: the garbage passage in Nan Yar answers whether one must inquire into the tattvas (categories of reality), not one's bad habits; the teach, myth and source wording were corrected to the categories. Also cut 'the question anyone who has tried to sit quietly ends up asking' and 'people tend to remember' as unsourced generalizations.
